title: It's a 'killing machine': Local advocates calling for Kinneytown Dam's deconstruction - NewsBreak
text: SEYMOUR, Conn. (WTNH) — A dam near Seymour that has been standing for nearly two centuries may be reaching the end of its lifespan, as locals and experts say it’s dangerous to the ecosystem. “This dam is a killing machine,” said local Kevin Zak. “I call it the Dam of Death” According to Paul Woodworth of Save the South, this particular dam blocks about 30 miles of mainstream habitat for migratory fish and has a considerable impact on the ecosystem. Formerly used to generate hydropower, the Kinneytown Dam no longer produces energy and has become a barricade for fish. “So, when dams like this prevent 30 miles of access to their former spawning grounds, it really shuts down the population,” Woodworth said. “The population basically collapses.” Woodworth says that the dam endangers multiple species of fish, such as alewife and American eel. These are both are food sources for birds and other fish, both inland and in the Long Island Sound. “It could result in wholesale die off of a lot of other species if we’re not careful enough and we can’t bring them back to a sustainable population size,” said Woodworth. The dam was originally built in 1844. Now, 180 years later, Save the Sound has spent the last three years along with their partners to raise $46 million for the dam’s deconstruction. “It’s no longer generating power and it’s no longer passing fish,” said Woodworth. One of the first people to ring the alarm bells was local Kevin Zak. “In a real selfish way, I loved being able to come down here and film,” said Zak. “But it’s got to go!” Zak says he has seen pools of dead sea lamprey and videoed crowds of fish unable to pass through the dam. “At times, I’d go back and talk to my wife, and I’d be in tears at what I saw,” he said. “It was the hill I was going to die on, literally. I’m 65, if it took me to 85 or 95 I was still going to fight to get rid of this thing.” Woodworth says that the $46 million of state and federal funding is just part of what they need. He hopes for the project to begin in 2027 and says the dam could be down in less than two years after they start. For the latest news, weather, sports, and streaming video, head to WTNH.com.
